content.title: This paper proposes a new semi-supervised domain adaptation method considering both feature and classifier adaptations and evaluates it against other methods on several datasets, with promising but not entirely convincing results.
content.review:
This paper proposes to learn invariant representations and risks (LIRR) for the semi-supervised domain adaptation problem, with theoretical analysis to back up the idea. Evaluation on experiments on multiple datasets shows the superiority of LIRR, with some insights provided. It is an interesting paper but I do have some concerns below:

1. Section 1 (par 2): The introduction reads like semi-supervised DA is a new(er) problem by focusing on recent literature. However, there is a rich literature on semi-supervised DA that have been ignored (many papers more than 10 years old) though I do see that unsupervised DA is popular today. As a recent post in twitter said, it is not good for science if we think literatures in the past 3-5 years are all/most we have. The so-called invariance representations and invariant risks appear in names such as feature adaptation and classifier adaptation in transfer learning/domain adaptation literature. Therefore, the main idea here is not that new actually. 

2. Will invariant representations and invariant risks be related (rather than independent)? The ablation study in Sec. 5.4 did not actually provide an ablation study directly on LIRR. It simply compares with other algorithms with different designs. A more proper ablation study should vary the LIRR model to study the differences, i.e. setting \lambda_{risk} = 0 and then \lambda_{rep} = 0, unless this will degenerate to other models compared. 

3. Notations are not always clear/consistent. In Eq. (4), should I(Y; D|Z) be I(D; Y|Z) instead? Also, ‘m’ denotes samples in 'T’ in Theorems 3.1 and 3.2. However, in Section 2 (page 3), 'm' denotes the number of labelled target samples “\tilde{T}” while k denotes the number of unlabelled target samples “T”. This is confusing and clarification is needed. If the definition of “m” in Sections 2 and 3 are consistent, then it seems that the generalisation bounds will not be affected by the number of unlabelled target samples “k”, which could be counterintuitive. 

4. The last paragraph of Section 3 says "Comparing with previous results (Ben-David et al., 2010; Zhao et al., 2019a), our bounds here contain empirical error terms from both the source and target domains." However, Theorem 3 in (Ben-David et al., 2010) also gives empirical risk minimization using combined source and target training data. It will be better to clarify further what are the specific differences here (Theorem 3.1 in this paper and Theorem 3 in Ben-David et al., 2010).

5. In Section 5.1, it says "For each dataset, we randomly pick source-target pairs for the evaluation". Why random? Have you repeated such random picking multiple times and will the results or conclusions vary? Why not conduct standard evaluation as in the literature? Later it says "we randomly select a small ratio (1% or 5%) of the target data". How many times has this been repeated?

6. I cannot find statistics on the datasets (even in the Appendix), e.g. for the NICO dataset, how many images are available and how many have been used in this paper?

7. There is a larger gap between LIRR and LIRR+CosC on the NICO dataset compared to results on other datasets. Moreover, LIRR has lower accuracy than MME on NICO consistently. Could you provide an explanation?

8. To help digest the presented tables, it will be better to provide some summary such as the average performance.
Comparing visualisation of representation learnt by different algorithms?

9. Table 2 says "Citycam" in bold, but this name is not used elsewhere. 

10. Figure 2 is impressive, but it will be better to see the average results over all pairs to draw a conclusion. 

11. Computational complexity is not analysed. 

12. The mass citations in Section 6 reduce readability.
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Response to Reviewer #3
content.comment:
### Q1: Relations towards previous studies.
It is true that invariant representation and invariant risk are not two novel terms, and they may derive from similar ideas in the existing literature. However, based on the discussion in recent studies [Zhao et al. 2019] and [Martin et al. 2019], our novelty comes from that we proposed an integrated learning objective for Semi-DA which is naturally derived from generalization bound analysis and the information theoretical interpretation.
### Q2: Ablation studies on $\lambda${risk} and $\lambda$_{rep}
We've done this ablation study already, but didn't set each of the terms to zero. However, we think it's really worth it, and we'll add this part of the experiment in our next revision version.
### Q3: Notations
In Eq. (4), $I(Y; D \mid Z)$ actually equals to $I(D; Y \mid Z)$ due to symmetrical characteristics of mutual information. For other clustered notations, we will improve them in our next revision.
### Q4: Discussions with previous theoretical analytical works.
Comparing with [Ben-David et al., 2010], we replace $\lambda$ term with our fourth term in Theorem 3.1 and Theorem 3.2, though it's a straightforward extension from [Zhao et al. 2019a]. We do not prefer to claim our work has novel insights in theoretical analysis comparing with [Zhao et al. 2019a, Zhao et al. 2019b, Combes et al. 2020], but we do provide a tighter bound both in classification and regression tasks in semi-da setting comparing with previous one. We will also add more discussions on existing works in our revision version.
### Q5, 6, 7, 8: Experimental Settings
We will make our experiment sections more clearly in our revised version. Because we did a lot of experiments on many tasks, datasets, it costs a lot of computing resources to evaluate all domain pairs in each dataset, so we only give certain domain pairs. Many of the works of UDA, Semi-DA also selected only a few domain pairs for comparison. For target labeled sampling, we repeat it 3 times and use fixed sampled target data for all the compared methods.
We will add more statistics about the datasets in our next revision. NICO is a relatively new dataset, we would add more explanations on how we evaluate our methods on this dataset.
As we pointed out in our paper, Cosine Classifier is a module with obvious performance gain in MME. And it can be added to our network as a plug-in module. After adding Cosine Classifier, our network has achieved considerable performance improvement, so LIRR+CosC can stably outperform MME in all evaluations.
Other Questions
For other questions, we would revise them in our revised version.

Arjovsky, Martin, et al. "Invariant risk minimization." arXiv preprint arXiv:1907.02893 (2019).

Ben-David S, Blitzer J, Crammer K, Kulesza A, Pereira F, Vaughan JW. A theory of learning from different domains. Machine learning. 2010 May 1;79(1-2):151-75.

Zhao H, Combes RT, Zhang K, Gordon G. On learning invariant representation for domain adaptation. arXiv preprint arXiv:1901.09453. 2019 Jan 27.

Zhao H, Coston A, Adel T, Gordon G. Conditional Learning of Fair Representations. In Proceedings of the 8th International Conference on Learning Representations, 2020.

Saito, Kuniaki, et al. "Semi-supervised domain adaptation via minimax entropy." Proceedings of the IEEE International Conference on Computer Vision. 2019.

content.title: There seems a gap between the proposed bound and the objective actually used. The contribution of the invariant risk part is not convincing enough.
content.review:
--------------------------
Summary:
This paper proposes a generalization upper bounds for both classification and regression problems under Semi-DA. This paper introduces a new method to learn invariant representations and risks under Semi-DA settings simultaneously. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. 

--------------------------
Pros:
1. The author proposes a generalization upper bound for Semi-DA works both for the classification and regression problems.
2. The invariant risk is introduced to help to align the conditional distributions.
3. Extensive experiments are conducted on both classification and regression tasks to demonstrate the proposed method's effectiveness.

--------------------------
Cons:
1. The bound is a naive extension from Ben-David's.
2. There is a gap between the proposed bound and the objective actually used, which should be clarified since the weighted sum of the empirical source and target error disappear from the final objective.
3. The main contribution, a.k.a, the invariant risk part, is not convincing enough. I can see from Eq.5 that the objective tries to find a consistently estimated classifier f_d for the worst feature space induced by feature extractor g through adversarial learning. However, it does not guarantee that optimal labeling functions are close to each other. To make it more convincing, the reviewer's suggestion is to show the feature space like MME at least and check whether the conditional distributions are better aligned. Or, simply learn the estimated classifiers \hat{f}_s, \hat{f}_t from the feature space obtained by the proposed method and compare their distance with other methods.
4. There should be more explanation about f_i and f_d, and the reviewer cannot find which one is actually used for the final prediction. Besides, an illustration of different f might be helpful.
5. Eq.5 is a little confusing. To my understanding, f_d can represent both f_s and f_t. If that's the case, it would be better to write it separately because there are actually two hypotheses trying to maximize the objective.
6. The paper mentions the problem brought by the imbalance label distributions, but I don't see any effort which is made to tackle the problem like PADA.

--------------------------
Reasons for Score:
Currently, the reviewer rates 5/10 due to my second and third concerns. If more convincing evidence is provided, the reviewer may raise the score.

content.title: Response to Reviewer #1
content.comment:
### Q1: The bound is a naive extension.
However, we do not agree that our bound is a naive extension from Ben-David's. We replace $\lambda$ term with our fourth term in Theorem 3.1 and Theorem 3.2, which is tighter than the $\lambda$ one. $\lambda$ depends on the choice of the hypothesis class \mathcal{H}, while our term does not. Though it's a straightforward extension from [Zhao et al. 2019a], we do not prefer to claim our work has novel insights in theoretical analysis comparing with [Zhao et al. 2019a, Zhao et al. 2019b, Combes et al. 2020], but we do provide a tighter bound both in classification and regression tasks in semi-da setting comparing with previous one. We will also add more discussions on existing works [Ben-david 2010, Redko et al. 2017, Redko et al. 2019] in our revision version.
### Q2,4,5: Gap between proposed bound and the objective actually used.
We will clarify our learning objective in Section 4.2 with more explanations and intuitions in our next revision version.
Here is a brief explanation about Eq. (5). We use $f_i$ to denote domain-invariant predictor, and $f_d$ to represent domain-dependent predictor. $f_i$ means the predictor is only aware of the representation $z$, while $f_d$ has additional information d to show z comes from source or target domain. 
In Eq. (5), $f_d$ does not represent both $f_S$ and $f_T$. $f_S$ and $f_T$ are two bayesian optimal classifiers in source and target domain; they are used as analytical tools in the theoretical analysis part. $f_d$ is an instantiated predictor which takes both representations $z$ and domain index d as input, we also term it as domain-dependent predictor. $f_i$ and $f_d$ are both trained on source and target labeled data, the only difference between them is that $f_i$ takes only representation $z$ as input, $f_d$ takes the combination of z and domain index d as input (we concatenate d as an additional channel in feature representation $z$). As the minmax notation suggests, both $f_i$ and $f_d$ aim at minimizing the training errors on sampled data (x, y). For $f_i$ and $f_d$, they should also be informative to take $g(x)$ and predict y.
After training, $f_d$ will be adopted and $f_i$ will be used for final prediction.
### Q3: The main contribution is the invariant risk part. 
I think there is a big misconception towards our usage for $f_d$ and our contribution. We do not only propose the learning invariant risks objective, but we provide an integrated optimization framework that can simultaneously learn invariant representations and invariant risks with sound theoretical proof and interpretation. Also, $f_d$ is not used as the final predictor, it is more used as an auxiliary predictor to help us learn the invariant predictor $f_i$. Eq. (5) can be intuitively known as approaching the minimization of H(Y \mid Z) - H(Y \mid D, Z), as well as achieving the predictions' invariance between $f_i$ and $f_d$ over the same representation $z$. If we take the example of binary classification of bear and dog as in Fig. 1, if $f_i$ and $f_d$ have their prediction of bear according to a proper representation of animal's shape, then any domain information will not contribute to the prediction, thus the predictor captures the invariant part and achieves invariant risks.
### Q6: Label Distribution Shifts
We mentioned in the abstract that the label distribution shift is a failure case of invariant representation learning, so we propose our method to learn invariant representations and risks altogether which avoids many potential problems when only using invariant representation as analyzed in [Zhao et al. 2019a].

Zhao H, Combes RT, Zhang K, Gordon G. On learning invariant representation for domain adaptation. arXiv preprint arXiv:1901.09453. 2019 Jan 27.

content.title: The theoretical contribution is incremental
content.review:
###############

Summary:
This paper proposes a theoretical analysis of semi-supervised domain adaptation, based on the theoretical results, a bound minimization algorithm, LIRR, to jointly learn invariant representations and invariant optimal predictors. Empirical results justify the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm. 

###############

Pros:
1.	This paper provides generalization bounds for semi-DA.
2.	The paper is overall well-written and easy to understand.
3.	Learning invariant risks (i.e., Eq. 5) is also interesting to me. From my perspective, this is the most significant (algorithmic) contribution of this work, though similar work has been investigated previously [Song et al. 2019, Steinberg et al. 2020].

Cons:
1.	My main concern is that the theoretical contribution of this paper is incremental. The authors claim that this is the first generalization analysis in the Semi-DA setting. In fact, some semi-supervised theoretical results have been analyzed previously (e.g. Theorem 3 of [Ben-david 2010], Theorem 3 of [Redko et al. 2017], and Theorem 5.7 of [Redko et al. 2019]). In addition, the theoretical analysis in this paper follows a standard set of steps that has been repeatedly adopted in several previous works (e.g., [Zhao et al. 2019a, Zhao et al. 2019b, Combes et al. 2020]), and didn’t provide any new insights. 
2.	The empirical evaluation protocol also seems problematic. Except for MME, the authors compared with lots of unsupervised oriented baselines where the target labels are totally inaccessible. Those methods were designed towards UDA rather than semi-DA, so they may not have good performance even though they were trained under a semi-DA mode. For a fair comparison, I would like to encourage the authors to compare some other approaches which are also trained under a semi-supervised mode, e.g. [Su et al. 2020] proposed the learner to actively select some target instances and retrain the model in a semi-supervised way. More comparison with semi-supervised approaches is needed.
3.	In this manuscript, the authors proposed to randomly select some portion of the target domain instances. However, previous work (e.g. [Su et al. 2020]) showed that random selection might not be a good choice. I’m curious that when the learner only has access to only a few instances in the target domain, will the model perform stable enough to the random choice? For example, in Table 1, in the art -> real-world task experiment on the office home dataset. There are ~4350 images in the target domain (real-world), if you only choose 1% of the target domain, which means you only have 44 images from the target domain. However, the number of classes in the office-home dataset is 65. This means this random selection could not cover all the target labels. I’m curious whether this imbalanced choice will have some negative impacts or not?
4.	This submission mentioned label distribution shifts several times, but I didn’t see any connection between label distribution shifts problems with this submission. Neither theoretical justifications nor empirical evaluations were conducted, which makes me feel confused by this submission.
5.	The authors claim that this paper provides finite-sample generalization bounds. However, the third and fourth terms in Thms 3.1 and 3.2 still rely on the expectation (and labeling functions) on the source and target domains.    
6.     Additional questions regarding (5): it seems that f_d in (5) is not defined, so it is not quite clear to me how to derive the second term Proposition 4.1. Additionally, in Proposition 4.1, the expectation is taken over Z, but in (5), it is taken over X, which is another issue of the derivation (but I think it could be fixed by data processing inequality).  The last issue is how to compute the expectation in (5). I believe that in practice the expectation is replaced by the mixture of the empirical source and target distributions. Since the size of the target data is very small, the prior probability of target data will also be very small. Do you use some over-sampling approach to re-balance the data?    

################

Overall:

Although I appreciate the idea of Learning Invariant Risks, I don’t think this paper does not meet the standard for an ICLR publication. I found very few novel theoretical insights from this paper. I encourage the authors to rethink the theoretical contributions and empirical justifications for a better one.

###############

References:

[Ben-David et al. 2010] Ben-David S, Blitzer J, Crammer K, Kulesza A, Pereira F, Vaughan JW. A theory of learning from different domains. Machine learning. 2010 May 1;79(1-2):151-75.

[Redko et al. 2017] Redko I, Habrard A, Sebban M. Theoretical analysis of domain adaptation with optimal transport. In Joint European Conference on Machine Learning and Knowledge Discovery in Databases 2017 Sep 18 (pp. 737-753). Springer, Cham.

[Su et al. 2020] Su JC, Tsai YH, Sohn K, Liu B, Maji S, Chandraker M. Active adversarial domain adaptation. In The IEEE Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision 2020 (pp. 739-748).

[Zhao et al. 2019a] Zhao H, Combes RT, Zhang K, Gordon G. On learning invariant representation for domain adaptation. arXiv preprint arXiv:1901.09453. 2019 Jan 27.

[Zhao et al. 2019b] Zhao H, Coston A, Adel T, Gordon G. Conditional Learning of Fair Representations. In Proceedings of the 8th International Conference on Learning Representations, 2020.

[Steinberg et al. 2020] Steinberg, D., Reid, A., O'Callaghan, S., Lattimore, F., McCalman, L. and Caetano, T., 2020. Fast Fair Regression via Efficient Approximations of Mutual Information. arXiv preprint arXiv:2002.06200.

[Redko et al. 2019] Redko, I., Morvant, E., Habrard, A., Sebban, M., & Bennani, Y. (2019). Advances in Domain Adaptation Theory. Elsevier.

[Steinberg et al. 2020] Steinberg, D., Reid, A., O'Callaghan, S., Lattimore, F., McCalman, L. and Caetano, T., 2020. Fast Fair Regression via Efficient Approximations of Mutual Information. arXiv preprint arXiv:2002.06200.

[Songet al. 2019] Song, J., Kalluri, P., Grover, A., Zhao, S. and Ermon, S., 2019, April. Learning controllable fair representations. In The 22nd International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics (pp. 2164-2173).

### Q1: Theoretical Contribution
Compared with traditional theoretical semi-supervised domain adaptation work[Ben-david et al. 2010], we replace $\lambda$ term with our fourth term in Theorem 3.1 and Theorem 3.2, which is tighter than the $\lambda$ one. $\lambda$ depends on the choice of the hypothesis class \mathcal{H}, while our term does not. We will add comparison experiments with [T Kim et al. 2020] and [Su et al. 2020] in our next revision version. However, we do not think that we are only comparing with the UDA method. The key point of our experiment is to compare with three types of methods (1) invariant representation (2) invariant risk (3) current state-of-art method. We believe that MME represents the latest approach with excellent performance, and we have surpassed them in the different tasks and datasets, so we can claim the effectiveness of LIRR.

Sorry for that we do not clarify it in our experimental setting, we will add this detail in our next revision version. content.review:
# Summary:
This paper works on semi-supervised domain adaptation (SSDA). It derives a finite-sample generalization bound for SSDA, for both classification and regression problems. This generalization bound then inspires the proposed LIRR algorithm to learn invariant features and risks. The authors conducted experiments for SSDA on multiple datasets. While the results and the algorithms look promising, there are many details unclear in the current manuscript and require further clarifications. 

# Strengths:
The paper derives a finite-sample generalization bound for SSDA, for both classification and regression problems. This generalization bound then inspires the proposed LIRR algorithm to learn invariant features and risks. The authors conducted experiments for SSDA on multiple datasets, for both the classification and regression problems.

# Weaknesses:
1. Ben-David’s seminal work and Zhao et al.’s work have already shown that (1) the difference in marginal distribution across domains and (2) how well a single classifier can work in both domains affects the performance of domain adaptation. With a slight amount of labeled target data, it seems straightforward to add (2) into the learning objective. Even in unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA), several existing works, such as CDAN, match the marginal and conditional distributions together. The authors should provide more discussions on this line of work.


2. The writing of sections 2, 3, and the use of notation can be improved.
- Theorem 3.1 and 3.2 do not differentiate the labeled (m) and unlabeled target (k) data. The “T” there should be \tilde{T}, as defined on page 3. The H-divergence terms remain the population bound.

- The use of notation can be improved. Specifically, the authors use S to represent the labeled source data and source domain, simultaneously. It is thus hard to tell if E_S is the expectation on the source data or on the source domain distribution. It is also hard to tell if f_S, f_T are the optimal classifiers on the source and target domain distributions or source and target domain data.


3. Several details of the proposed approach are not clear.
- Eq. (6) seems to not involve the terms that minimize the empirical errors on the source and target labeled data, as stated in Theorem 3.1 and Theorem 3.2. There are no definitions of f_i and f_d in (5) and (6). It is unclear what is the final classifier being trained. Note that, if Eq. (5) is to approximate I(Y;D|Z) whose min value is 0, then a trivial solution for (5) is a constant function f_i and f_d (i.e., always predict 1 or 0).

- It is still unclear why the fourth term in Theorem 3.1 and Theorem 3.2 can be replaced by I(Y ;D| Z). Note that, Theorem 3.1 and Theorem 3.2 involve the optimal classifiers which are unknown.


4. Experiments:
- While the authors experimented on multiple datasets, for each dataset they only evaluate a few pairs of domains. For example, in MME (Saito, 2019), more than 7 pairs on DomainNet and Office-Home are evaluated, and here the authors only show 3.

- The authors didn’t compare to some recent methods in SSDA, which have outperformed MME and maybe the proposed methods.

C. Qin et al., Opposite structure learning for semi-supervised domain adaptation, arxiv, 2020

L. Yang et al., MiCo: Mixup Co-Training for Semi-Supervised Domain Adaptation, arxiv 2020

T. Kim et al., Attract, Perturb, and Explore: Learning a Feature Alignment Network for Semi-supervised Domain Adaptation, ECCV 2020.

While some of them are recent arXiv papers, a discussion and a comparison to them would strengthen the paper.

- It is unclear how the authors extend the baseline methods initially proposed for UDA to SSDA. The reported accuracies of MME are much worse than those in (Saito, 2019).

- As mentioned in Theorem 3.1 and 3.2, they are four terms that can be optimized. I would like to see an ablation study on the effects of these four terms in the proposed algorithm.

- The implementation details in the main paper is insufficient. The authors only describe the network architecture in the appendix.


5. Others:
- The related work on existing SSDA algorithms is insufficient. See above.

- It seems that both Ben-David et al. and Zhao et al. have both provided a finite sample bound. Could the authors provide more discussions on this? Also, a recent work [A] has also provided abound with labeled target information. Could the authors discuss this?

[A] J. Wu and J. He, Continuous Transfer Learning with Label-informed Distribution Alignment, arXiv 2020.


# Minor comments:
- I would recommend that the authors provide more intuitions on Eq. (5). Specifically, what are the two loss terms trying to learn?

- I would suggest that the author uses SSDA instead of semi-DA for abbreviation.

- There seems no definition on the function f on page 2. I think it is the labeling function.

- In deriving the bound, the authors seem to assume that the feature function "g" is fixed. However, it will be learned in the proposed algorithm. Will this affect the bound?

# Justification:
While the paper presents a new finite-sample bound for SSDA and presents a new algorithm for SSDA, similar concepts of the combination of feature and risk invariance has been proposed in UDA. Besides, some details of the proposed algorithms are not clear, especially that the empirical risks are not added to the learning objective. The experiments are not comprehensive --- only partial results are reported for benchmark datasets like DomainNet and office-home. There are also no ablation studies on the use of different loss terms. I thus give a score of 4.

content.title: Response to Reviewer #2
content.comment:
Thanks for your valuable comments.
### Q1: Comparisons with existing theoretical study

LIRR should not be considered as simply adding (2) as our learning objective over previous seminal works in UDA. We consider our proposed network as simultaneously learning invariant representations and risks. The integrated objective, if interpreting with information theory, is to achieve the joint independence over $D \perp Y, Z$, which consists of achieving marginal independence of $D \perp Z$ and conditional independence $D \perp Y | Z$. We do not think the conditioning objective in CDAN shares similarity with ours learning invariant risks, as CDAN’s learning objective focuses on achieving the invariant conditional representation of $Pr(Z | Y)$ across domains. While invariant risk focuses on achieving the invariance of $Pr(Y | Z)$ across domains if we can find the proper representation $Z$. There have been some existing works on causal invariant prediction [Jonas et al., 2015] or invariant risk minimization [Martin et al. 2019] discussed the invariant learning objective. We are inspired by them yet still different, IRM achieves the objective via gradient penalty with a dummy classifier, but our objective is learned by the difference of domain-invariant predictor's cross-entropy and domain-dependent predictor's cross-entropy.

Peters, Jonas, Peter Bühlmann, and Nicolai Meinshausen. "Causal inference by using invariant prediction: identification and confidence intervals." Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B (Statistical Methodology) 5.78 (2016): 947-1012.

Arjovsky, Martin, et al. "Invariant risk minimization." arXiv preprint arXiv:1907.02893 (2019).

### Q2: Notations can be further improved
Thanks for your suggestions. We would improve our notations to avoid misconceptions in our revision.
### Q3: Details of the proposed method are not clear
Thanks for pointing this out, we would add more details about $f_i$ and $f_d$ in Section (4.2) in further revision versions. But we think there are misconceptions of our objectives in Eq. (5) and Eq. (6).
$f_i$ and $f_d$ are both trained on source and target labeled data, the only difference between them is that $f_i$ takes only representation $z$ as input, $f_d$ takes the combination of z and domain index d as input. As the min-max notation in Eq.(5) suggests, both $f_i$ and $f_d$ aim at minimizing the training errors on sampled data (x, y).
We did not directly use $f_i$ and $f_d$ to represent $f_S$ and $f_T$ as in Theorem 3.1 and Theorem 3.2. $f_S$ and $f_T$ are the optimal bayesian predictor in source and target domain, $f_i$ and $f_d$ are instantiated objectives. $f_i$ aims at taking $g(x)$ as input which does not consider domain difference, hence we term it as domain-invariant predictor. $f_d$ aims at taking both $g(x)$ and domain index d as input, hence we term it as domain-dependent predictor. In each training iteration, the two predictors take the same batch of input $x$ and output the corresponding prediction y, but $f_d$ with an additional domain index information d. 
The difference of two predictors intuitively suggests the impact of domain information. If the difference is 0, that means our predictor conditions on the proper part of representation which gives the invariant prediction across domains (e.g. to predict bear, if the predictors only consider shape information, then they will give invariant predictions whether the $f_d$ has an additional domain index information).
As the reviewer suggests, simply minimizing the loss difference between $f_i$ and $f_d$ will potentially result in the trivial solution: $g(x)$ is irrelevant with both input $x$ and domain index d, that means $g(x)$ is a random output from the encoder. But this won’t actually happen in the optimization process, the loss of $f_i$ will be always greater than $f_d$, since $f_d$ has more information, even at the initial stage. But for clarity and absolute correctness, we will rewrite it into a clearer form.

content.title: Response to Reviewer #2
content.comment:
### Q4: Experiments
We don’t consider our experimental results lacking confidence for we did not do enough pairs of experiments on one dataset. For example, there are 30 pairs of experiments in total on DomainNet, which is a very large and infeasible number. Current works, like [‘MME’, ‘Attract, Perturb and Explore’],  or other work in UDA setting [DANN, ADDA, SE, ADR, CAN], seldom actually do all of the pairs on any of the dataset. 
Apart from this, we've done experiments on two types of tasks, more than any classical method or SOTA method [‘DANN’, ‘IRM’, ‘MME’, ‘Attract, Perturb and Explore’], including image classification and traffic counting (which is a regression task). For image classification tasks, we have more experiments on different datasets than any other existing Semi-DA works. With regard to evaluating how many pairs in one dataset, we don't think it was an issue with our experimental setting, nor did MME experiment all pairs on DomainNet.
Also, It is worth noting that our setting and MME are not exactly the same so we do not have to compare with MME on its specifically defined setting. The 1-shot and 3-shot sampled target labeled data in MME are not enough to measure the real data distribution in the target domain, so we use 1% and 3% target labeled data, which is more than the 1-shot and 3-shot data in most of the datasets. For the case that 1% and 3% of samples are not enough to guarantee at least one sample for each class, we will also force to increase the total number of samples to satisfy at least one sample for each class.
For the lack of and existing methods, we'll consider comparison with ["Attract, Perturb and Explore"] in our revision version. For other papers that are still undergoing peer review, we will consider conducting experimental comparison after they are officially accepted.
### Q5: Minor Comments
We will consider to give more explanations and examples in Section 4.2 and give more intuitions of Eq. (5). We do not consider the feature transformation 'g' is fixed, 'g' is the most important component in our network since we expect it captures the most important semantics information that induces invariant representations and invariant risks (predictions) across domains. It would be learned during the optimization procedure with the proposed learning objective.

replying_to: Replying to Learning Invariant Representations and Risks for Semi-supervised Domain Adaptation

content.title: General Response
content.comment:
We thank all the reviewers for their valuable comments. We would like to first provide a general response to some common misconceptions of the reviewers as below, and then reply to the detailed questions from each reviewer separately.
### Learning Objective of LIRR
We would like to point out there are some misconceptions from the reviewers of our final learning objective. We clarify our learning objective in Section 4.2 with more explanations and intuitions in the revised version. 

Here we would like to provide a brief explanation of Eq. (5). We use $f_i$ to denote domain-invariant predictor, and $f_d$ to represent domain-dependent predictor. $f_i$ means the predictor is only aware of the representation $z$, while $f_d$ has additional information d to demonstrate that z comes from source or target domain. $f_i$ and $f_d$ are both trained on source and target labeled data, the only difference between them is that $f_i$ takes only representation $z$ as input, $f_d$ takes the combination of z and domain index d as input (we concatenate d as an additional channel in feature representation $z$). 

The difference of two predictors intuitively suggests the impact of domain information. If the difference is 0, that means our predictor conditions on the proper part of representation which gives the invariant prediction across domains (e.g. to predict bear, if the predictors only consider shape information, then they will give invariant predictions whether the $f_d$ has an additional domain index information).

In Eq. (5), $f_d$ does not represent both $f_s$ and $f_t$, where $f_s$ and $f_t$ are two bayesian optimal classifiers in source and target domain; they are used as analytical tools in the theoretical analysis part. As the minmax notation suggests, both $f_i$ and $f_d$ aim at minimizing the training errors on sampled data $(x, y)$. For $f_i$ and $f_d$, they should also be informative to take $g(x)$ and predict y. 

As R2 points out, simply minimizing the loss difference between $f_i$ and $f_d$ will potentially result in the trivial solution that $g(x)$ is irrelevant with both input $x$ and domain index d, that means $g(x)$ is a random output from the encoder. But this won’t actually happen in the optimization process, the loss of $f_i$ will be always greater than $f_d$, since $f_d$ has more information, even at the initial stage. But for clarity and absolute correctness, we will rewrite it into a clearer form.

After training, $f_d$ will be adopted and $f_i$ will be used for final prediction. 
### Theoretical Improvement with Previous DA works
Compared with traditional theoretical semi-supervised domain adaptation work [Ben-david et al. 2010], we replace $\lambda$ term with our fourth term in Theorem 3.1 and Theorem 3.2, which is tighter than the $\lambda$ one. $\lambda$ depends on the choice of the hypothesis class \mathcal{H}, while our term does not. Though it's a straightforward extension from [Zhao et al. 2019a], we do not prefer to claim our work has novel insights in theoretical analysis comparing with [Zhao et al. 2019a, Zhao et al. 2019b, Combes et al. 2020], but we do provide a tighter bound both in classification and regression tasks in semi-da setting comparing with previous one. We will also add more discussions on existing works [Ben-david 2010, Redko et al. 2017, Redko et al. 2019] in our revised version.
### Experimental Settings
For the lack of comparison with existing methods, we'll consider comparison with ["Attract, Perturb and Explore"] in our revision version. For other papers that are still undergoing peer review, we will consider conducting experimental comparison after they are officially accepted.
Apart from this, we do not consider our experimental results lacking confidence since we've done experiments on two types of tasks, including image classification and traffic counting (which is a regression task). For image classification tasks, we have more experiments on different datasets than any other existing Semi-DA works.
Also, It is worth noting that our setting and MME are not exactly the same so we do not have to compare with MME on its specifically defined setting. The 1-shot and 3-shot sampled target labeled data in MME are not enough to measure the real data distribution in the target domain, so we use 1% and 3% target labeled data, which is more than the 1-shot and 3-shot data in most of the datasets. 
For the case that 1% and 3% of samples are not enough to guarantee at least one sample for each class, we will also force to increase the total number of samples to satisfy at least one sample for each class.
Finally, we consider adding more explanatory experiments and visualization results for better understanding our proposed method. Our implementation of LIRR and experimental benchmark will be released soon.

content.comment:
We have uploaded a revised version of our paper, where we made substantial modifications based on the suggestions from the reviews. Below is the list of changes:

1. We have improved the notations in section 2 and section 3, as well as in theorem 4.2 and 4.3, to make them consistent and tidy.

2. We have added more descriptive texts in section 4.2 to make it easier to understand. We would like to point out that our learning objective in the original version is correct, but the reviewer may have misunderstandings due to lack of explanation. In the revised version, we have added more explanatory descriptions to build better connections between Eq. (4) and Eq. (5), as well as for better understanding of the learning objective of LIRR.

3. We have provided more discussions and comparisons on the existing theoretical studies on semi-supervised domain adaptation. 

4. We have added more explanatory descriptions in the experimental section, especially for the latest proposed dataset NICO.
